title: Check yourself: syntax and usage of text blocks

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A query is declared as `String sql = """   // totals per region`, followed by a line `SELECT region, SUM(total) FROM orders GROUP BY region` and a line holding only `""";`. What does javac 21 do with it?

options.text: It accepts the declaration and leaves the comment out of the value, since javac drops a comment wherever it appears in the source
options.says: only white space and a line terminator may follow the opening delimiter; a comment is not allowed there, and javac reports a missing line terminator

options.text: It accepts the declaration and starts the value with the comment text, since the value begins right after the opening delimiter
options.says: content never starts on the opener's line; javac refuses the line instead of keeping the text

options.text: It reports its first error at the opening delimiter, since nothing but white space may come between that delimiter and the end of its line
options.says: the opening delimiter must be followed by optional white space and a line terminator; anything else, a comment included, is an error

options.text: It reports its first error at the closing delimiter, since a closing delimiter has to follow the last content on that content's own line
options.says: the first error is on the opener's line; in a well-formed text block a closing delimiter on its own line is legal and only adds a final newline

origin.section: The Opening Delimiter Ends Its Line, So Even One Line of Text Takes Two

questions.stem: A test writes the expected CSV as a text block with the three lines `id,qty`, `7,2` and `9,1`, and puts the closing delimiter on a line of its own below them. The code under test returns the same three rows with `\n` between them and none after the last. What do `expected.equals(actual)` and `expected.lines().count()` give?

options.text: `equals` is false and the count is 3, since the fixture has a line break after `9,1` that the returned string lacks
options.says: a closing delimiter on its own line ends the value with \n; lines() does not count a final line break as starting a new line

options.text: `equals` is false and the count is 4, since the line break after `9,1` opens an empty fourth line
options.says: lines() treats a final terminator as the end of the last line, so both values hold three lines

options.text: `equals` is true and the count is 3, since the closing delimiter's line is layout and adds nothing to the value
options.says: the closing delimiter on its own line leaves a \n after the last content line, so the values differ by one character

options.text: `equals` is true and the count is 4, since the closing delimiter's line is read as an empty fourth line that `equals` ignores
options.says: the closing delimiter's line adds a \n to the value, which equals sees; lines() never counts a final terminator as starting a new line

origin.section: The Closing Delimiter's Line Decides Whether the Value Ends With a Newline

questions.stem: `static final String ACTIVE` is a text block holding `ACTIVE`, and `isActive(String status)` returns `status == ACTIVE`. The unit tests call `isActive("ACTIVE")`; in production the status comes from `resultSet.getString("status")`. What happens?

options.text: Both the tests and production get true, since equal strings all resolve to the one pooled instance of the text block
options.says: only constants share the pooled instance; a string the driver builds at run time is a separate object

options.text: Both the tests and production get false, since a text block is a different object from the quoted literal with its characters
options.says: a text block is the same compile-time constant as the equal literal, so the test's comparison is true

options.text: Only the tests get true, since the literal is the same pooled object as the constant and the driver's string is a new one
options.says: constants are interned and identical; a string built at run time has the same characters but is another object, so == is false

options.text: Only production gets true, since the driver hands back pooled strings and the test's literal is a copy of its own
options.says: the literal is the pooled constant, and a string built at run time is a separate object

origin.section: A Text Block Is a Compile-Time Constant, the Same Object as the Equal Literal

questions.stem: With `static final int YEAR = 2026;`, a team tries two declarations of `static final String REPORT` for use as `case REPORT ->` in a switch on a String: (1) a text block holding `REPORT`, then `+ " " + YEAR`; (2) a text block holding `REPORT %d`, then `.formatted(YEAR)`. Which compile as the label?

options.text: Only (1), since a text block joined with `+` to constants is still a constant expression
options.says: + between constants keeps a compile-time constant; a method call such as formatted() never is one

options.text: Only (2), since javac evaluates `formatted` when every argument is a constant
options.says: formatted() runs in the static initializer; javac reports 'constant string expression required' for the label

options.text: Both, since each one is a `static final` String built only from constants
options.says: static final is not enough: the initializer must be a constant expression, and a method call is not

options.text: Neither, since a text block is not a literal that a `case` label accepts
options.says: a text block is a compile-time constant like a quoted literal, so it can be a case label

origin.section: A Text Block Is a Compile-Time Constant, the Same Object as the Equal Literal

concepts: A text block is a compile-time constant, the same pooled object as the equal literal, while a string built at run time is a separate object.
A text block joined with + to constants stays a constant and can be a case label; one with formatted() is computed at run time and cannot.
lines() counts the same lines whether or not the value ends with a newline, while equals and a hash see the difference.
Only white space may follow the opening delimiter before its line terminator; content or a comment on that line does not compile.
